Internet Connectivity and Students' Learning Experience at NSUK¶

Course: NS-DTS 223 Data Exploration and Visualization, Group Practical Assignment Topic 2: Internet Connectivity and Students' Learning Experience on Campus Institution: Nasarawa State University, Keffi (NSUK)

This notebook runs the full analysis on the group's survey data: inspection → audit → cleaning → EDA → analysis → visual data story → recommendations. It follows Stages 1–5 of the assignment brief. Every cleaning decision is logged and every figure is saved to reports/figures/.

Stage 1: Problem identification and planning¶

Problem statement. Students rely more and more on the internet for lecture materials, research, online classes, portal tasks and assignment submission. If campus connectivity is poor or unreliable, this learning gets disrupted. The study looks at how students on the NSUK campus experience internet connectivity, and how that experience relates to their academic activities.

Central storytelling question.

How do students experience internet connectivity across the NSUK campus, and how is a poorer connectivity experience associated with disruption to their learning?

Analytical (research) questions

# Question Story stage
RQ1 How do students access the internet on campus (network provider, connection type, frequency of academic use)? Overview
RQ2 How does the connectivity experience differ across the campus locations where students go online, and across providers? Pattern / distribution
RQ3 At what times of day do students report the best connection? Pattern / trend
RQ4 Is a poorer connectivity rating associated with a greater perceived effect on academic performance? Relationship
RQ5 Are students with poorer connectivity more likely to have missed an academic deadline because of it? Key insight
RQ6 What improvements do students want the university to make? Recommendation

Target population: registered NSUK students (all levels and faculties) who use the internet on the Keffi campus. Sampling technique: non-probability convenience sampling. The online questionnaire (Google Forms) was shared through student channels. Expected sample size: ≥ 100 valid responses (the brief's target). Achieved: 84 (see limitations). Intended audience: university management and ICT/Works directorates, the Students' Union, and mobile network operators serving the campus. Collection period: 18–22 November 2026 (from the form timestamps). Ethics: participation was voluntary and anonymous. No names, matriculation numbers, phone numbers or e-mails were collected.

4. Data quality audit¶

The inspection above is turned into a systematic audit. Each check is computed from the data, not assumed, so it can be re-run if more responses arrive.

In [7]:
SINGLE = {6: "freq_use", 8: "rating", 9: "poor_freq", 11: "disconnect", 12: "satisfaction", 15: "impact"}
MULTI_BY_DESIGN = {4: "provider", 10: "best_time", 13: "affected_activity", 18: "uni_should"}
def q(n): return QTEXT[n]
def is_multi(s): return s.astype(str).str.contains(",", regex=False) & s.notna()

audit = []
def add(check, column, n, detail, action):
    audit.append({"check": check, "column": column, "rows_affected": int(n), "finding": detail, "planned_action": action})

# Missing values
for i in range(1, 21):
    n = raw[q(i)].isna().sum()
    if n: add("Missing value", f"Q{i}", n, f"{n} blank answer(s)",
              "Keep row; leave as NaN and analyse with available-case n" if i < 19 else "Optional open question; NaN = no comment")
# Mixed coding in Q8
num = raw[q(8)].astype(str).str.fullmatch(r"\d")
first_num = raw.loc[num, "Timestamp"].min()
add("Inconsistent coding", "Q8", num.sum(),
    f"{num.sum()} answers are digits 1-5, the rest are text labels; digits appear only from {first_num:%d %b %H:%M} (form edited mid-collection)",
    "Map 1-5 to Very poor ... Excellent after validating direction")
# Multi-answers in single-choice questions
for i in SINGLE:
    n = is_multi(raw[q(i)]).sum()
    if n: add("Multiple answers to single-choice item", f"Q{i}", n,
              "; ".join(raw.loc[is_multi(raw[q(i)]), q(i)].unique()),
              "Adjacent options -> keep the one nearer the scale midpoint; contradictory options -> NaN")
# Department free text
d = raw[q(3)].dropna()
add("Inconsistent free-text categories", "Q3", d.size,
    f"{d.nunique()} raw spellings collapse to {d.str.strip().str.lower().nunique()} after trimming/lower-casing (e.g. 'Computer science', 'Computer Science ', 'Computer')",
    "Trim, standardise spelling, map to canonical department names")
# Faculty-department mismatch
mm = (raw[q(2)] == "Social Sciences") & raw[q(3)].astype(str).str.contains("Microbiology", case=False)
add("Logical inconsistency", "Q2/Q3", mm.sum(), "Microbiology reported under Faculty of Social Sciences",
    "Correct faculty to Natural and Applied Sciences (department is the more specific answer); flag row")
# Trailing commas in checkbox items
for i in (13, 18):
    n = raw[q(i)].astype(str).str.strip().str.endswith(",").sum()
    if n: add("Formatting artefact", f"Q{i}", n, "Trailing comma in checkbox answer", "Strip before splitting")
# Contradictory Q10
c10 = raw[q(10)].astype(str)
n10 = (c10.str.contains("No noticeable") & c10.str.contains(",")).sum()
add("Contradictory multi-select", "Q10", n10, "'No noticeable difference' ticked together with a specific time slot",
    "Keep the specific time slot(s), drop the 'no difference' flag; record in log")
# Implausible level
n500 = (raw[q(1)] == "500 Level").sum()
add("Plausibility", "Q1", n500, "500 Level respondent in Computer Science (a 4-year programme)",
    "Cannot be verified; retain (could be an extra year) and note")
# Non-informative text
JUNK = r"^\s*(yes|no|non|none|nil|nothing|a lot|n/?a|hardworking)\s*\.?\s*$"
for i in (19, 20):
    n = raw[q(i)].astype(str).str.lower().str.match(JUNK).sum()
    add("Non-informative text", f"Q{i}", n, "Answers such as 'Yes', 'Non', 'Nil', 'A lot'", "Flag as non-informative; exclude from theme coding")
# Duplicates / outliers / sample
add("Duplicates", "all", raw.drop(columns="Timestamp").duplicated().sum(), "No duplicate submissions found", "None required")
add("Outliers", "all", 0, "All items are categorical/ordinal with fixed options, so there are no out-of-range numeric values. Spend (Q17) is banded",
    "Screen ordinal extremes and response patterns instead (Section 6.3)")
add("Sample coverage", "Q2", (raw[q(2)] == "Natural and Applied Sciences").sum(),
    f"{(raw[q(2)]=='Natural and Applied Sciences').mean():.0%} of respondents are from one faculty; n = {len(raw)} < 100 target",
    "Report as limitation; compare NAS vs other faculties only descriptively")
audit = pd.DataFrame(audit)
audit.to_csv(TAB / "data_quality_audit.csv", index=False)
audit

18 Logical inconsistency Q2/Q3 1 Microbiology reported under Faculty of Social Sciences Correct faculty to Natural and Applied Sciences (department is the more spec...
19 Formatting artefact Q13 2 Trailing comma in checkbox answer Strip before splitting
20 Contradictory multi-select Q10 4 'No noticeable difference' ticked together with a specific time slot Keep the specific time slot(s), drop the 'no difference' flag; record in log
21 Plausibility Q1 1 500 Level respondent in Computer Science (a 4-year programme) Cannot be verified; retain (could be an extra year) and note
22 Non-informative text Q19 3 Answers such as 'Yes', 'Non', 'Nil', 'A lot' Flag as non-informative; exclude from theme coding
23 Non-informative text Q20 5 Answers such as 'Yes', 'Non', 'Nil', 'A lot' Flag as non-informative; exclude from theme coding
24 Duplicates all 0 No duplicate submissions found None required
25 Outliers all 0 All items are categorical/ordinal with fixed options, so there are no out-of... Screen ordinal extremes and response patterns instead (Section 6.3)
26 Sample coverage Q2 65 77% of respondents are from one faculty; n = 84 < 100 target Report as limitation; compare NAS vs other faculties only descriptively

Audit summary. The raw file has 84 responses × 21 columns with no duplicate submissions. Problems requiring action:

  1. Mixed coding in Q8. From 20 Nov onwards, 31 ratings were recorded as digits 1–5 instead of text labels. This shows the form was edited during collection.
  2. Single-choice items with more than one answer (8 cells across Q6, Q8, Q9, Q12, Q15). The form allowed ticking several boxes on Likert items.
  3. Department free text. 27 raw spellings (differing in case, spacing and abbreviation) covering 19 real departments, plus 6 blanks.
  4. One faculty–department contradiction, trailing commas in checkbox items, and 4 contradictory Q10 answers (No noticeable difference ticked together with a specific time).
  5. Non-informative open text (e.g. "Yes", "Non", "Nil") in Q19/Q20.
  6. Coverage. n = 84 is below the 100 target, and 77% of raw respondents (79% after one faculty correction) come from one faculty. This is a limitation, not something cleaning can fix.

No respondent is dropped. Every problem can be fixed in place, and the few missing answers are handled with available-case analysis (each statistic reports its own n).

5. Data cleaning and preparation¶

All transformations go through a log() helper, so the cleaning log (reports/tables/cleaning_log.csv) is generated by the cleaning code itself rather than written up afterwards.

5.1 Rename columns and add a respondent ID¶

In [8]:
CLEAN_LOG = []
def log(step, column, rows, action, rationale):
    CLEAN_LOG.append({"step": len(CLEAN_LOG) + 1, "stage": step, "column": column,
                      "rows_affected": int(rows), "action": action, "rationale": rationale})

NAMES = ["timestamp", "level", "faculty", "department", "provider_raw", "connection_type", "freq_use",
         "access_location", "rating", "poor_freq", "best_time_raw", "disconnect", "satisfaction",
         "affected_activity_raw", "effect_type", "impact", "missed_deadline", "weekly_spend",
         "uni_should_raw", "challenge_text", "suggestion_text"]
df.columns = NAMES
df.insert(0, "respondent_id", [f"R{i:03d}" for i in range(1, len(df) + 1)])
log("Structure", "all", len(df), "Renamed 21 question columns to short snake_case names; added respondent_id R001-R084",
    "Readable, code-friendly names; stable anonymous key")

# Trim whitespace in all text columns
txt = df.select_dtypes(include=["object", "string"]).columns
before = df[txt].copy()
df[txt] = df[txt].apply(lambda s: s.map(lambda v: re.sub(r"\s+", " ", v).strip() if isinstance(v, str) else v))
changed = (before.fillna("") != df[txt].fillna("")).any(axis=1).sum()
log("Standardise", "all text", changed, "Trimmed leading/trailing spaces and collapsed repeated spaces",
    "e.g. 'Computer science ' and 'Computer science' were counted separately")
df["timestamp"] = pd.to_datetime(df["timestamp"])
df["collection_date"] = df["timestamp"].dt.date

5.3 Ordinal coding and single-choice items with more than one answer¶

Questions 6, 8, 9, 11, 12 and 15 are single-choice Likert-type items, yet a few respondents ticked two options (the form appears to have allowed checkboxes). Rule applied consistently:

  • Adjacent options (e.g. Good, Average): keep the option nearer the scale midpoint. This is the conservative choice, because it does not exaggerate either extreme.
  • Non-adjacent / contradictory options (e.g. Very satisfied, Very dissatisfied): set to missing, since the true answer cannot be recovered.

Each item then gets a numeric _code (1–5) for statistics, and its text label is kept as an ordered categorical.

In [10]:
SCALES = {
    "freq_use":     ["Never", "Rarely", "Sometimes", "Very often", "Always"],
    "rating":       ["Very poor", "Poor", "Average", "Good", "Excellent"],
    "poor_freq":    ["Never", "Rarely", "Sometimes", "Often", "Always"],
    "disconnect":   ["Never", "Rarely", "Sometimes", "Often", "Always"],
    "satisfaction": ["Very dissatisfied", "Dissatisfied", "Neutral", "Satisfied", "Very satisfied"],
    "impact":       ["Not at all", "Slightly", "Moderately", "Highly", "Very highly"],
}
def resolve(val, scale):
    if pd.isna(val): return np.nan, None
    parts = [p.strip() for p in str(val).split(",") if p.strip()]
    codes = [scale.index(p) + 1 for p in parts]
    if len(codes) == 1: return codes[0], None
    if max(codes) - min(codes) >= 2: return np.nan, "contradictory -> NaN"
    keep = min(codes, key=lambda c: abs(c - 3));  return keep, f"adjacent -> '{scale[keep-1]}'"

df["flag_multi_single"] = ""
for col, scale in SCALES.items():
    res = df[col].apply(lambda v: resolve(v, scale))
    df[f"{col}_code"] = res.str[0].astype("Int64")
    notes = res.str[1]
    for kind in ("adjacent", "contradictory"):
        m = notes.fillna("").str.startswith(kind)
        if m.any():
            log("Resolve multi-answer", col, m.sum(),
                "; ".join(f"'{a}' {b.split(' ',1)[1]}" for a, b in zip(df.loc[m, col], notes[m])),
                "Adjacent: keep option nearer midpoint (conservative). Contradictory: unrecoverable -> NaN")
            df.loc[m, "flag_multi_single"] += f"{col};"
    df[col] = pd.Categorical(df[f"{col}_code"].map(lambda c: scale[c-1] if pd.notna(c) else np.nan),
                             categories=scale, ordered=True)

SPEND = ["Below ₦1,000", "₦1,000–₦2,000", "₦2,001–₦3,000", "₦3,001–₦5,000", "Above ₦5,000"]
df["weekly_spend"] = pd.Categorical(df["weekly_spend"], categories=SPEND, ordered=True)
df["weekly_spend_code"] = (df["weekly_spend"].cat.codes + 1).astype("Int64")
LEVELS = ["100 Level", "200 Level", "300 Level", "400 Level", "500 Level"]
df["level"] = pd.Categorical(df["level"], categories=LEVELS, ordered=True)
df["level_num"] = df["level"].cat.codes.add(1).mul(100).astype("Int64")
df["missed_deadline_bin"] = df["missed_deadline"].map({"Yes": 1, "No": 0}).astype("Int64")
log("Data type", "level, weekly_spend, missed_deadline", len(df),
    "Converted to ordered categoricals with numeric codes (level 100-500, spend 1-5, deadline 0/1)",
    "Correct types allow sorting, medians and rank correlations")
pd.DataFrame(CLEAN_LOG).tail(7)

5.5 Checkbox (multi-select) questions → indicator columns¶

Q4 (provider), Q10 (best time), Q13 (affected activities) and Q18 (what the university should do) allow several answers. Each is split into 0/1 indicator columns. A tidy long table is also saved for frequency analysis. For these items, percentages are % of respondents and can sum to more than 100%.

In [12]:
def split_multi(s):
    return s.fillna("").astype(str).str.strip().str.rstrip(",").apply(
        lambda x: [p.strip() for p in x.split(",") if p.strip()])

TRAIL = df["affected_activity_raw"].astype(str).str.endswith(",") | df["uni_should_raw"].astype(str).str.endswith(",")
log("Standardise", "affected_activity, uni_should", TRAIL.sum(), "Removed trailing commas before splitting", "Formatting artefact")

def slug(x): return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "_", x.lower()).strip("_")
long_tables, MULTI_COLS, OPT_LABEL = [], {}, {}
for col, prefix in [("provider_raw", "prov"), ("best_time_raw", "time"),
                    ("affected_activity_raw", "act"), ("uni_should_raw", "uni")]:
    lists = split_multi(df[col])
    if prefix == "time":   # contradictory 'No noticeable difference' + specific slot
        bad = lists.apply(lambda L: "No noticeable difference" in L and len(L) > 1)
        lists = lists.apply(lambda L: [x for x in L if x != "No noticeable difference"] if len(L) > 1 else L)
        df["flag_time_contradiction"] = bad
        log("Resolve contradiction", "best_time", bad.sum(),
            "Dropped 'No noticeable difference' where a specific time slot was also ticked",
            "A named slot is the more informative answer")
    opts = sorted({o for L in lists for o in L})
    MULTI_COLS[prefix] = []
    for o in opts:
        name = f"{prefix}_{slug(o)}"
        df[name] = lists.apply(lambda L: int(o in L)).where(df[col].notna()).astype("Int64")
        MULTI_COLS[prefix].append(name); OPT_LABEL[name] = o
    df[f"{prefix}_n_selected"] = lists.str.len().where(df[col].notna()).astype("Int64")
    lt = df[["respondent_id"]].assign(option=lists).explode("option").dropna()
    lt.insert(1, "question", col.replace("_raw", "")); long_tables.append(lt)
log("Derive", "prov_*, time_*, act_*, uni_*", len(df), "Split 4 checkbox questions into 0/1 indicator columns + count of options ticked",
    "Multi-select answers cannot be analysed as a single category")

# Derived single-value versions
df["primary_provider"] = np.where(df["prov_n_selected"] > 1, "Multiple SIMs",
                                  df["provider_raw"].str.strip())
df["best_time_single"] = split_multi(df["best_time_raw"]).apply(
    lambda L: L[0] if len(L) == 1 else ("Multiple slots" if len(L) > 1 else np.nan))
df.loc[df["flag_time_contradiction"], "best_time_single"] = split_multi(
    df.loc[df["flag_time_contradiction"], "best_time_raw"]).apply(
    lambda L: [x for x in L if x != "No noticeable difference"]).apply(lambda L: L[0] if len(L) == 1 else "Multiple slots")
log("Derive", "primary_provider", (df["prov_n_selected"] > 1).sum(),
    "Respondents naming >1 provider coded 'Multiple SIMs'", "Keeps one provider category per student for grouping")
long_df = pd.concat(long_tables, ignore_index=True)
df.filter(like="prov_").sum()

5.6 Open-ended text: non-informative answers and theme coding¶

In [13]:
JUNK = r"^\s*(yes|no|non|none|nil|nothing|a lot|n/?a|hardworking)\s*\.?\s*$"
for col in ("challenge_text", "suggestion_text"):
    junk = df[col].astype(str).str.lower().str.match(JUNK) & df[col].notna()
    df[f"{col}_informative"] = df[col].notna() & ~junk
    log("Flag", col, junk.sum(), "Flagged non-informative answers (e.g. 'Yes', 'Non', 'Nil', 'A lot')",
        "Kept in data but excluded from theme coding")

CHALLENGE_THEMES = {
    "Slow speed":                    r"slow|speed",
    "No / weak signal, dead zones":  r"no signal|no internet|hardly have network|disappear|go blank|poor network|bad network|poor service|bad internet|terrible network|very poor",
    "Drops & instability":           r"instab|unstable|trip off|si[zr]e|failure|drops|unavailable|unexpected",
    "Online classes disrupted":      r"online class",
    "Research, downloads, videos":   r"research|download|video|file",
    "Exams, portal, assignments":    r"exam|portal|assignment|submit",
    "Calls & messaging":             r"\bcall|whatsapp",
    "Congestion / overload":         r"congest|thousands|bandwidth|multiple devices|traffic",
    "Location-specific (faculty, LT, hostel)": r"faculty|lt1|lt ?2|lecture hall|hostel|department|enter the campus",
    "Wi-Fi access":                  r"wi-?fi",
}
SUGGESTION_THEMES = {
    "More Wi-Fi / hotspots":            r"wi[-_ ]?fi|hotspot|hospot|router",
    "Starlink / satellite":             r"starlink",
    "Partner with telecom providers":   r"partner|network providers|telecom",
    "Affordable or free access":        r"afford|free|loan|broke|enough data",
    "Improve network infrastructure":   r"infrastructure|restore|network masses|more network|better network|fast network|network issues|faculty network",
    "Speed & reliability":              r"fast|speed|stab|reliab|strong",
    "Campus-wide / faculty coverage":   r"faculty|faculties|every corner|all round|across|all times",
}
def code_themes(col, themes, prefix):
    ok = df[f"{col}_informative"]
    for t, pat in themes.items():
        df[f"{prefix}_{slug(t)}"] = (df[col].str.contains(pat, case=False, regex=True) & ok).astype(int).where(ok).astype("Int64")
    return pd.Series({t: df.loc[ok, f"{prefix}_{slug(t)}"].sum() for t in themes}).sort_values(ascending=False)

ch = code_themes("challenge_text", CHALLENGE_THEMES, "chal")
sg = code_themes("suggestion_text", SUGGESTION_THEMES, "sugg")
log("Derive", "chal_*, sugg_*", df["challenge_text_informative"].sum() + df["suggestion_text_informative"].sum(),
    "Keyword-based theme coding of open-ended answers (one answer can carry several themes)",
    "Turns free text into countable evidence; dictionary shown in notebook for transparency")
display(ch.rename("challenge mentions").to_frame(), sg.rename("suggestion mentions").to_frame())

5.7 Derived analytical variables¶

Connectivity Experience Index (CEI). No speed-test data were collected, so the respondent's connectivity experience is summarised by combining the four perception items:

Item Direction
Q8 rating of connection (1 Very poor → 5 Excellent) higher = better
Q9 frequency of poor connectivity (1 Never → 5 Always) reversed
Q11 frequency of unexpected disconnection (1 Never → 5 Always) reversed
Q12 satisfaction with provider speed (1 Very dissatisfied → 5 Very satisfied) higher = better

CEI = mean of the four oriented items, rescaled to 0 (worst) – 100 (best). It requires at least 3 of the 4 items. Internal consistency is checked in Section 6.2.

Connectivity group (from Q8, for clear categorical comparison): Poor (Very poor/Poor), Average, Good (Good/Excellent). High academic impact: Q15 = Highly or Very highly.

In [14]:
items = pd.DataFrame({
    "rating": df["rating_code"].astype(float),
    "poor_freq_rev": 6 - df["poor_freq_code"].astype(float),
    "disconnect_rev": 6 - df["disconnect_code"].astype(float),
    "satisfaction": df["satisfaction_code"].astype(float),
})
df["cei"] = ((items.mean(axis=1) - 1) / 4 * 100).where(items.notna().sum(axis=1) >= 3).round(1)
df["conn_group"] = pd.Categorical(df["rating_code"].map({1: "Poor", 2: "Poor", 3: "Average", 4: "Good", 5: "Good"}),
                                  categories=["Poor", "Average", "Good"], ordered=True)
df["high_impact"] = df["impact_code"].map(lambda c: np.nan if pd.isna(c) else int(c >= 4)).astype("Int64")
df["cei_band"] = pd.cut(df["cei"], [-0.1, 40, 60, 100], labels=["Weak (≤40)", "Fair (40–60)", "Strong (>60)"])
log("Derive", "cei, conn_group, high_impact, cei_band", len(df),
    "Created Connectivity Experience Index (0-100), 3-level connectivity group, binary high-impact flag",
    "Summarise connectivity experience; enable group comparisons")
df[["respondent_id", "rating", "poor_freq", "disconnect", "satisfaction", "cei", "conn_group"]].head()

6. Validation of cleaning decisions¶

6.1 Is the 1–5 recoding of Q8 in the right direction?¶

If 1 meant Excellent (reversed), numeric-coded ratings would correlate negatively with satisfaction and positively with frequency of poor connectivity, which is the opposite of the text-labelled group. The two coding periods are compared below.

In [15]:
chk = []
for fmt, g in df.groupby("rating_format"):
    for other in ("satisfaction_code", "poor_freq_code", "disconnect_code"):
        sub = g[["rating_code", other]].dropna().astype(float)
        r, p = stats.spearmanr(sub.iloc[:, 0], sub.iloc[:, 1])
        chk.append({"Q8 format": fmt, "n": len(sub), "correlated with": other.replace("_code", ""), "Spearman rho": round(r, 2), "p": round(p, 3)})
chk = pd.DataFrame(chk); display(chk)
display(df.groupby("rating_format")["rating"].value_counts().unstack().fillna(0).astype(int))
Q8 format n correlated with Spearman rho p
0 numeric (1-5) 31 satisfaction 0.44 0.014
1 numeric (1-5) 31 poor_freq -0.64 0.000
2 numeric (1-5) 31 disconnect -0.55 0.002
3 text label 51 satisfaction 0.79 0.000
4 text label 53 poor_freq -0.43 0.001
5 text label 52 disconnect -0.25 0.077
rating Very poor Poor Average Good Excellent
rating_format
numeric (1-5) 5 4 17 2 3
text label 3 8 20 16 6

Result. In the numeric-coded group, Q8 correlates positively with satisfaction (ρ = 0.44) and negatively with frequency of poor connectivity (ρ = −0.64) and disconnection (ρ = −0.55). These are the same directions as in the text-labelled group. The mapping 1 = Very poor … 5 = Excellent is therefore confirmed.

Caveat: the numeric period has proportionally more Average answers (17 of 31, 55%, vs 20 of 53, 38%). A bare 1–5 scale often pulls answers to the midpoint, so this format change is listed as a limitation.

6.2 Internal consistency of the Connectivity Experience Index¶

In [16]:
def cronbach_alpha(x):
    x = x.dropna(); k = x.shape[1]
    return k / (k - 1) * (1 - x.var(ddof=1).sum() / x.sum(axis=1).var(ddof=1)), len(x)
alpha, n_alpha = cronbach_alpha(items)
print(f"Cronbach's alpha (4 items, n={n_alpha}): {alpha:.2f}")
item_total = {c: stats.spearmanr(items[c], items.drop(columns=c).mean(axis=1), nan_policy="omit")[0] for c in items}
print("Corrected item-total (Spearman):", {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in item_total.items()})
print("Alpha if item deleted:", {c: round(cronbach_alpha(items.drop(columns=c))[0], 2) for c in items})

Cronbach's alpha (4 items, n=81): 0.78
Corrected item-total (Spearman): {'rating': np.float64(0.63), 'poor_freq_rev': np.float64(0.62), 'disconnect_rev': np.float64(0.48), 'satisfaction': np.float64(0.57)}
Alpha if item deleted: {'rating': np.float64(0.69), 'poor_freq_rev': np.float64(0.71), 'disconnect_rev': np.float64(0.78), 'satisfaction': np.float64(0.73)}

Result. Cronbach's α = 0.78, which is acceptable internal consistency for a short perception scale (≥ 0.70). All four items correlate with the rest of the scale (item–total ρ = 0.48–0.63). Removing the disconnection item would not raise α (it stays 0.78), so all four items are kept for content coverage. The CEI can be treated as one summary of the connectivity experience.

6.3 Unusual observations (outlier screening for ordinal data)¶

In [17]:
# 1) CEI outliers by Tukey fences
q1, q3 = df["cei"].quantile([.25, .75]); iqr = q3 - q1
lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
print(f"CEI Tukey fences: [{lo:.1f}, {hi:.1f}] -> outliers:", df.loc[(df.cei < lo) | (df.cei > hi), "respondent_id"].tolist())
# 2) Internally inconsistent answer patterns
pat = df[((df.rating_code == 5) & (df.poor_freq_code == 5)) | ((df.rating_code == 1) & (df.poor_freq_code <= 2)) |
         ((df.impact_code >= 4) & (df.missed_deadline == "No") & (df.rating_code >= 4))]
print("Respondents with contradictory pattern (e.g. Excellent rating but 'Always' poor connection):", len(pat))
display(pat[["respondent_id", "rating", "poor_freq", "disconnect", "satisfaction", "impact", "missed_deadline"]])
# 3) Straight-lining across the oriented items
straight = (items.nunique(axis=1) == 1) & items.notna().all(axis=1)
print("Identical answer on all 4 oriented CEI items:", straight.sum())
df["flag_pattern_check"] = df["respondent_id"].isin(pat["respondent_id"])
log("Flag", "flag_pattern_check", df["flag_pattern_check"].sum(), "Flagged internally contradictory answer pattern; retained",
    "No basis to say which answer is wrong; sensitivity is negligible for 1 of 84 rows")

CEI Tukey fences: [-3.9, 102.4] -> outliers: []
Respondents with contradictory pattern (e.g. Excellent rating but 'Always' poor connection): 1
respondent_id rating poor_freq disconnect satisfaction impact missed_deadline
34 R035 Excellent Always Always Satisfied Highly Yes 
Identical answer on all 4 oriented CEI items: 13

Result. Because every item has fixed answer options, there are no impossible values, and the CEI has no Tukey outliers. One respondent (R035) gives an internally contradictory pattern: an Excellent rating while experiencing poor connectivity and disconnections Always. This is flagged (flag_pattern_check) but kept, because there is no basis for deciding which answer is wrong, and one row in 84 does not change any result. Thirteen respondents gave the same answer on all four oriented items, usually the middle option. This is a plausible "neutral" profile rather than careless straight-lining, so these rows are also kept.

def freq(s, order=None, name=None):
    vc = s.value_counts(dropna=False)
    if order is not None: vc = vc.reindex([o for o in order if o in vc.index] + [i for i in vc.index if i not in order])
    out = pd.DataFrame({"n": vc, "%": (vc / vc.sum() * 100).round(1)})
    out.index = out.index.map(lambda x: "Missing" if pd.isna(x) else x); out.index.name = name or s.name
    return out
profile = {c: freq(df[c]) for c in ["level", "faculty", "dept_group", "primary_provider", "connection_type", "access_location"]}

9. Exploratory data analysis: bivariate and multivariate¶

9.1 Connectivity experience across subgroups¶

Non-parametric tests are used because CEI is bounded and built from ordinal items, and some groups are small: Mann–Whitney U for two groups and Kruskal–Wallis H for three or more, with ε² / rank-biserial effect sizes. With n = 84 these tests have limited power, so effect sizes and medians are interpreted alongside p-values.

In [27]:
def compare(group, data=df, min_n=5):
    d = data[[group, "cei"]].dropna(); d = d[d[group].astype(object).map(d[group].astype(object).value_counts()).astype(int) >= min_n]
    g = d.groupby(group, observed=True)["cei"]
    tab = g.agg(n="size", median="median", mean="mean", IQR=lambda s: s.quantile(.75) - s.quantile(.25)).round(1).sort_values("median")
    samples = [s.values for _, s in g]
    if len(samples) == 2:
        U, p = stats.mannwhitneyu(*samples); eff = 1 - 2 * U / (len(samples[0]) * len(samples[1])); test = f"Mann-Whitney U={U:.0f}, p={p:.3f}, rank-biserial r={eff:.2f}"
    else:
        H, p = stats.kruskal(*samples); eps = (H - len(samples) + 1) / (len(d) - len(samples)); test = f"Kruskal-Wallis H={H:.2f}, p={p:.3f}, ε²={max(eps,0):.2f}"
    return tab, test, p
results = []
for grp in ["access_location", "primary_provider", "connection_type", "level", "faculty_group", "dept_group", "weekly_spend"]:
    tab, test, p = compare(grp); results.append({"grouping": grp, "test": test, "p": round(p, 3)})
    print(f"\n### CEI by {grp}  ->  {test}"); display(tab)
subgroup_tests = pd.DataFrame(results); subgroup_tests.to_csv(TAB / "subgroup_tests_cei.csv", index=False)

Interpretation. None of the subgroup differences in CEI is statistically significant at α = 0.05, and the effect sizes are small:

  • Location (p = 0.60): medians range only from 43.8 (faculty buildings, library, lecture halls) to 56.2 ("Other"), and every location has a wide spread. A poor experience is not confined to one place.
  • Provider (p = 0.24): MTN, Glo and Airtel users have almost identical medians. Students carrying multiple SIMs score lowest (median 40.6, n = 10). This fits a picture of switching SIMs to cope with poor service, but the group is small.
  • Faculty (p = 0.076) and weekly spend (p = 0.057) are borderline. Students outside NAS and those spending less report somewhat poorer experiences, and the top spenders (> ₦5,000) the best (median 56). These are worth testing with a larger, more balanced sample.

Small groups (lecture halls n = 6, hostels n = 5, Campus Wi-Fi n = 8) limit statistical power, so a non-significant result here means "no clear evidence of a difference", not "proof of no difference".

9.2 Cross-tabulations and tests of association¶

In [28]:
def xtab(a, b, normalize="index"):
    ct = pd.crosstab(df[a], df[b]); pct = pd.crosstab(df[a], df[b], normalize=normalize).mul(100).round(1)
    chi2, p, dof, exp = stats.chi2_contingency(ct); V = np.sqrt(chi2 / (ct.values.sum() * (min(ct.shape) - 1)))
    small = (exp < 5).mean()
    return ct, pct, f"χ²({dof})={chi2:.2f}, p={p:.3f}, Cramér's V={V:.2f}; {small:.0%} of expected counts <5", p
for a, b in [("conn_group", "missed_deadline"), ("conn_group", "high_impact"), ("connection_type", "conn_group"),
             ("primary_provider", "conn_group"), ("access_location", "conn_group")]:
    ct, pct, s, p = xtab(a, b); print(f"\n### {a} x {b}: {s}"); display(pd.concat({"count": ct, "row %": pct}, axis=1))
# Fisher exact for the 2x2 key comparison: Poor vs Good/Average on missed deadline
tmp = df.dropna(subset=["missed_deadline_bin"]).assign(poor=lambda d: (d.conn_group == "Poor").astype(int))
t22 = pd.crosstab(tmp.poor, tmp.missed_deadline_bin); OR, pF = stats.fisher_exact(t22)
print(f"\nFisher exact (Poor vs Average/Good x missed deadline): OR={OR:.2f}, p={pF:.3f}"); display(t22)

Interpretation.


    

  • Connectivity rating × high academic impact: significant (χ²(2) = 10.48, p = 0.005, Cramér's V = 0.36, a moderate association). 65% of students with a Poor connection report high impact, compared with about 25% in the Average and Good groups.
    •

  • Connection type and provider show no clear association with the rating. The location × rating test returns p = 0.042, but 56% of its expected counts are below 5, so the χ² approximation is unreliable. Together with the non-significant CEI test above, it is not treated as evidence of a location effect.

9.3 Correlation analysis (Spearman rank correlation)¶


















In [29]:






CORR_VARS = {"level_num": "Level", "freq_use_code": "Academic use", "rating_code": "Rating (Q8)",
             "poor_freq_code": "Poor conn. freq (Q9)", "disconnect_code": "Disconnection freq (Q11)",
             "satisfaction_code": "Satisfaction (Q12)", "impact_code": "Academic impact (Q15)",
             "missed_deadline_bin": "Missed deadline (Q16)", "weekly_spend_code": "Weekly spend (Q17)", "cei": "CEI"}
C = df[list(CORR_VARS)].astype(float).rename(columns=CORR_VARS)
rho = C.corr(method="spearman")
pval = pd.DataFrame(np.ones(rho.shape), index=rho.index, columns=rho.columns)
for i in rho.index:
    for j in rho.columns:
        if i != j:
            sub = C[[i, j]].dropna(); pval.loc[i, j] = stats.spearmanr(sub[i], sub[j])[1]
rho.round(2).to_csv(TAB / "spearman_matrix.csv", encoding="utf-8-sig")
key_pairs = (rho.where(np.triu(np.ones(rho.shape), 1).astype(bool)).stack().rename("rho").to_frame()
             .join(pval.stack().rename("p")).assign(abs=lambda d: d.rho.abs()).sort_values("abs", ascending=False).drop(columns="abs").round(3))
display(key_pairs.head(15))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 7.5))
rh, pv = rho.iloc[1:, :-1], pval.iloc[1:, :-1]
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(rh, dtype=bool), k=1)
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("mono", ["#F7FAFA"] + SEQ)
sns.heatmap(rh.abs(), mask=mask, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=1, annot=rh, fmt=".2f", annot_kws={"size": 8.5},
            linewidths=2, linecolor=SURF, cbar_kws={"shrink": .7, "label": "Strength |Spearman ρ| (sign shown in cell)"}, ax=ax)
for t, v in zip(ax.texts, rh.abs().values[~mask]): t.set_color(SURF if v > .55 else INK)
for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(pv.values):
    if j <= i and v < .05: ax.text(j + .5, i + .82, "•", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK)
ax.set_title("Correlation between connectivity and academic-impact measures"); ax.grid(False)
subtitle(ax, "Spearman rank correlation, pairwise n. Shade = strength; negative values mean the measures move in opposite directions. • = p < 0.05")
save(fig, "eda_05_correlation_heatmap")

Interpretation. As expected, the four CEI components correlate strongly with the CEI (|ρ| 0.70–0.82) and moderately with one another. Of the academic-impact measures:


    

  • Disconnection frequency is the strongest correlate of perceived academic impact (ρ = 0.36, p = 0.001). Being cut off unexpectedly seems to matter more to students than general speed.
    • 

  • Better connectivity experience goes with lower perceived impact (CEI ρ = −0.31, p = 0.005; rating ρ = −0.28, p = 0.009).
    • 

  • Perceived impact and missed deadlines move together (ρ = 0.31, p = 0.005), which supports the consistency of the responses.
    • 

  • Heavier academic use goes with higher weekly data spend (ρ = 0.41). Students who depend more on the internet pay more for it.
    • 



These correlations are moderate. They show association, not causation.

# Partial Spearman: CEI vs impact controlling for weekly spend and level (rank-based residual method)
R = C[["CEI", "Academic impact (Q15)", "Weekly spend (Q17)", "Level", "Academic use"]].dropna().rank()
def resid(y, X): X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X]); return y - X @ np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
ctrl = R[["Weekly spend (Q17)", "Level", "Academic use"]].values
pr, pp = stats.pearsonr(resid(R["CEI"].values, ctrl), resid(R["Academic impact (Q15)"].values, ctrl))
print(f"Partial Spearman CEI vs academic impact | spend, level, academic use: rho={pr:.2f}, p={pp:.3f}, n={len(R)}")

Interpretation. Of the 62 students who named a time slot, 45% say night (8 PM onwards) gives the best connection, well ahead of evening (26%), morning (21%) and afternoon (19%). Another 22 students (26% of all) notice no difference. This fits daytime congestion, when most students and staff are on campus at once, an explanation several students also gave in their open answers ("Hundreds or thousands of students… connecting multiple devices"). Night is when students are least able to attend classes or reach campus facilities, so the best connectivity comes at the least useful time for scheduled learning.
























10. Visual data story¶
The figures below form one narrative that follows the brief's structure: Overview → Pattern/Distribution → Pattern over time → Relationship → Key insight → Recommendation. Chart types follow the suggestions for Topic 2 (bar, box plot, line, heatmap) plus a grouped bar for the key insight. Every chart uses one colour family (teal): lighter tones for context, the darkest tone for the point being made.






















The story in one sentence: NSUK students depend heavily on the internet for learning but mostly rely on their own mobile data. Their connectivity experience is middling across the whole campus and best only at night, and students with poorer connectivity report much greater harm to their academic work, which points to campus-wide, daytime connectivity as the priority.

Why this chart: a bar chart is the clearest way to compare the share of students in each category (RQ1). Providers are a multi-select item, so bars show % of respondents and can add up to more than 100%.


Finding: 82% of students rely mainly on their own mobile data, and only 10% mainly use campus Wi-Fi. MTN is the most used network (54%), followed by Glo (32%) and Airtel (27%), and 12% carry more than one SIM. With 89% using the internet Very often/Always for academic work, students' learning depends heavily on commercial mobile networks that they pay for themselves.

Finding: the CEI medians sit between 44 and 56 in every location, mostly at or below the scale midpoint, and the boxes overlap heavily (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.60). fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.8))

sns.heatmap(hm, cmap=seq_cmap, vmin=0, vmax=60, annot=hm_n.astype(str).where(hm_n > 0, ""), fmt="", annot_kws={"size": 10},
            linewidths=2, linecolor=SURF, cbar_kws={"label": "% of row (rating group)", "format": mtick.PercentFormatter()}, ax=ax)
for t in ax.texts:
    t.set_color(SURF if float(hm.values.flat[ax.texts.index(t)]) > 38 else INK)
ax.set_yticklabels([f"{l}  (n={n})" for l, n in zip(hm.index, rn.values)], rotation=0)
ax.set_xlabel("Q15 Perceived effect of poor connectivity on academic performance"); ax.set_ylabel("Q8 Rating of campus connection")
ax.set_title("Students who rate their connection poorly report a greater academic impact")
subtitle(ax, f"Shade = % of rating group, number = students.  Spearman ρ(rating, impact) = {r_:.2f} (p = {p_:.3f});  ρ(CEI, impact) = {r2:.2f} (p = {p2:.3f})")
ax.grid(False); save(fig, "story_04_rating_vs_impact_heatmap")
















































Why this chart: a heatmap shows how two ordinal variables are jointly distributed (RQ4). Shading is by row percentage, so rating groups of different sizes can be compared, and the cell numbers keep the underlying counts visible.


Finding: the darkest cells run from upper-right to lower-left. Students rating their connection Very poor cluster at Very highly affected (4 of 8), and Poor raters cluster at Highly (6 of 12). Good/Excellent raters cluster at Slightly/Moderately, and none of them reports Very high impact. The rank correlation is negative and significant (ρ = −0.28 for the single rating, −0.31 for the CEI), and it holds after adjusting for spend, level and usage (partial ρ = −0.28, p = 0.011).

Why this chart: a grouped bar chart compares two outcome rates side by side across three ordered connectivity groups (RQ5).


Key insight:


    

  • Students who rate their connection Poor are 2.6 times as likely as everyone else to say their academic performance is highly affected (65% vs 25%, χ² p = 0.005).
    • 

  • Missed deadlines are widespread: 71% of all respondents have missed at least one because of poor connectivity, including 59% of those who rate their connection Good. The rate is highest in the Poor group (85%), but the gradient is not statistically significant at this sample size.
    • 



Two messages follow. Poor connectivity is associated with the greatest academic harm, and deadline losses affect most students whatever their usual connection quality. Occasional failures at critical moments seem to be enough.

Finding: students' own priorities match the evidence. The top requests in the closed question are more Wi-Fi hotspots (50%) and better existing infrastructure (40%), followed by partnering with telecom providers and affordable access (29% each). The open answers repeat this: more Wi-Fi and hotspots, coverage in every faculty, Starlink/satellite (5 mentions), and speed and reliability.
























11. Conclusions, recommendations and limitations¶
11.1 Answers to the research questions¶




RQ
Answer (evidence)






RQ1: Access
82% rely on personal mobile data; only 10% use campus Wi-Fi. MTN is the most used network (54%). 89% use the internet very often/always for academic work, and 65% spend over ₦3,000 per week on data.




RQ2: Where
The connectivity experience is middling (median CEI 44/100) in all locations. Location and provider differences are small and not significant, so the problem is campus-wide.




RQ3: When
Night is most often reported as the best time (45%), and the afternoon least (19%). This is consistent with daytime congestion.




RQ4: Relationship
Poorer connectivity goes with greater perceived academic impact (ρ = −0.31, p = 0.005), and this holds after controlling for spend, level and use. Disconnections are the strongest single correlate (ρ = 0.36).




RQ5: Key insight
Poor-connectivity students are 2.6× as likely to report high academic impact (65% vs 25%). 71% of all students have missed a deadline because of connectivity.




RQ6: What students want
More Wi-Fi hotspots (50%), better infrastructure (40%), telecom partnerships and affordable access (29% each).






11.2 Evidence-based recommendations¶




#
Recommendation
For
Supporting evidence






1
Expand campus Wi-Fi as a campus-wide service, starting with academic spaces (faculty buildings, FNAS LT1/LT2, library, lecture halls), with enough capacity for daytime peaks.
University management, ICT
Only 10% use campus Wi-Fi; 50% request hotspots; poor experience in every location; location-specific dead zones are the 2nd most common open-text complaint




2
Negotiate capacity upgrades with MTN, Glo and Airtel (extra cell sites or small cells, and capacity for daytime peaks on campus).
Management, network operators
52% experience poor connectivity often/always; best quality reported at night; disconnection frequency is the strongest correlate of academic impact




3
Make learning more resilient to connectivity failures: record online classes, make materials downloadable for offline use, and allow grace periods or alternative submission routes when outages happen near deadlines.
Lecturers, departments, Senate
71% have missed a deadline; online classes (49%) and research (46%) are the most affected activities




4
Reduce students' data costs: pursue zero-rated access to the student portal, LMS and e-library, and student data bundles through operator partnerships.
Management, Students' Union, operators
65% spend over ₦3,000 per week; 82% depend on their own data; 29% request affordable access




5
Monitor connectivity objectively: run scheduled speed tests at fixed locations and times each semester, and publish a simple dashboard.
ICT directorate
This study relies on perceptions; objective data would confirm where and when to invest






11.3 Limitations¶
    

  • Sample size and representativeness: n = 84 (below the 100 target), from a convenience sample. 79% of respondents are NAS students and 87% are 200–300 Level, so results are indicative and not campus-wide estimates.
    • 

  • Self-reported measures only: no network speed tests or direct observation were carried out, although the brief suggests them for this topic. Connectivity is measured as perceived experience.
    • 

  • Instrument changes during collection: Q8 switched from labels to a 1–5 scale, and some single-choice items accepted several ticks. Both were resolved with documented rules, but the format change may have pushed some Q8 answers toward Average.
    • 

  • Associational design: cross-sectional survey data cannot show causation. For example, students who struggle academically for other reasons may also blame connectivity more readily.
    • 

  • Multiple testing: about 20 significance tests were run. The main findings (p ≤ 0.011) are robust, but borderline results (p ≈ 0.05–0.08) should be treated as hypotheses.
    • 

  • Open-text coding uses a transparent keyword dictionary. It is approximate, and a few long answers read like generic or AI-assisted text.
    •
